key_terms.meaning: Only one normal stress is non-zero (σx ≠ 0, σy = σz = τ = 0), as in a bar pulled by an axial force.
Two normal stresses act on perpendicular faces (σx and σy) while the third normal stress and all shears on the third face are zero.
Normal and shear stresses act on all three faces; the general state at a point inside a loaded body.
The part of the stress tensor with equal normal stresses σm = (σx+σy+σz)/3; it changes volume only.
Stress tensor minus its spherical part; it changes shape and drives yielding.
A plane inclined at angle θ to a face on which the given stresses act; stresses on it are found from force equilibrium.

key_terms.term: Normal stress on an inclined plane
key_terms.meaning: σn = (σx+σy)/2 + ((σx−σy)/2)cos2θ + τxy sin2θ, in N/mm².

key_terms.term: Shear stress on an inclined plane
key_terms.meaning: τ = −((σx−σy)/2)sin2θ + τxy cos2θ, in N/mm²; sign depends on the convention chosen.
σx + σy = σ1 + σ2 at a point; the sum of normal stresses does not change when axes rotate.
The two perpendicular planes, at angle θp, on which the shear stress is zero.
σ1, σ2 = (σx+σy)/2 ± √(((σx−σy)/2)² + τxy²); the largest and smallest normal stresses at the point.
τmax = √(((σx−σy)/2)² + τxy²) = (σ1 − σ2)/2; acts on planes at 45° to the principal planes.
Circle with centre C = ((σx+σy)/2, 0) and radius R = τmax; each point on it gives stress on one plane.
ε1,2 = (εx+εy)/2 ± √(((εx−εy)/2)² + (γxy/2)²); the shear strain enters halved.
Three strain gauges fixed at known angles (0°–45°–90° or 0°–60°–120°) on one spot to give εx, εy and γxy.
Failure occurs when σ1 reaches the yield strength; safe if σ1 ≤ σy/FOS. Used for brittle materials.
Yielding starts when τmax = (σ1 − σ2)/2 reaches σy/2; safe if σ1 − σ2 ≤ σy/FOS. Used for ductile materials.
Equivalent stress σ′ = √(σ1² − σ1σ2 + σ2²) must stay below σy/FOS; matches ductile test data best.
εx = ∂u/∂x, εy = ∂v/∂y, γxy = ∂u/∂y + ∂v/∂x; strains come from gradients of displacements u and v.
∂σx/∂x + ∂τxy/∂y + X = 0 and its partner; they link how stresses change from point to point under body force X.

takeaways: A stress state at a point is fully fixed by the normal and shear components on three mutually perpendicular faces, and its simplest labels are uniaxial, biaxial and triaxial.
Stresses on a plane tilted by θ vary with 2θ, so the complete picture repeats every 180° of rotation.
When axes rotate, the normal stresses change but their sum does not; this invariant equals σ1 + σ2.
Principal planes carry zero shear and carry the largest and smallest normal stresses at the point.
The maximum in-plane shear stress equals half the difference of the principal stresses and sits 45° from the principal planes.
Mohr's circle converts the transformation equations into one drawing whose centre gives the mean stress and whose radius gives the maximum shear.
Strains transform exactly like stresses, except that the shear strain appears as γ/2 in every equation.
Three strain gauges at known angles supply the three unknowns εx, εy and γxy, enough for principal strains and then principal stresses through Hooke's law.
A failure theory reduces a complex stress state to one number that is compared with the yield strength to give a factor of safety.
Tresca and von Mises suit ductile metals, Rankine suits brittle materials; the choice of theory can change the safe size of a part.
Equilibrium equations and strain-displacement relations together give the field description of a deforming body, with compatibility closing the set.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for a derivation of the inclined-plane or principal-stress equations followed by a numerical case, and for a comparison of Rankine, Tresca and von Mises with a factor-of-safety calculation.

bank.q: Define a stress state at a point. Sketch and explain uniaxial, biaxial and triaxial states, and split the general triaxial tensor into spherical and deviatoric parts.
outline: Stress components on three perpendicular faces fix the state
Uniaxial: one normal stress, example of an axially loaded bar
Biaxial: σx and σy act, example of a thin pressure vessel surface element
Triaxial: all components act, example of a point inside a thick body
Mean stress σm = (σx+σy+σz)/3 is the spherical part; the remainder is deviatoric
Spherical part changes volume, deviatoric part changes shape

bank.q: Derive the expressions for normal and shear stress on a plane inclined at θ to the x-face of a body under plane stress.
outline: Take a wedge element cut by the inclined plane
Resolve forces normal to and along the plane
Use area of inclined face = area of vertical face / cos θ
Obtain σn = (σx+σy)/2 + ((σx−σy)/2)cos2θ + τxy sin2θ
Obtain τ = −((σx−σy)/2)sin2θ + τxy cos2θ
State sign convention and note dependence on 2θ

bank.q: State the plane stress transformation equations for σx′, σy′ and τx′y′ and prove that σx + σy is invariant under rotation.
outline: Write the three transformation equations in terms of 2θ
Add the first two equations
The cos2θ and sin2θ terms cancel
Conclude σx + σy = σx′ + σy′ = σ1 + σ2
Mention this is the first stress invariant

bank.q: Explain the construction of Mohr's circle for plane stress and show how principal stresses, principal planes and maximum shear stress are read from it.
outline: Plot point A(σx, τxy) and B(σy, −τxy)
Line AB is a diameter; centre lies on the σ axis at (σx+σy)/2
Radius R = √(((σx−σy)/2)² + τxy²)
Extremes on σ axis give σ1 and σ2
Top and bottom of circle give ±τmax and the 45° planes
Angle on the circle is 2θ; note the direction of rotation

bank.q: At a point in a machine part, σx = 120 N/mm², σy = 40 N/mm² and τxy = 60 N/mm². Find the principal stresses, the principal planes and the maximum in-plane shear stress.
outline: Use σ1,2 = (σx+σy)/2 ± √(((σx−σy)/2)² + τxy²)
Mean = 80 N/mm², radius = 72.1 N/mm²
σ1 = 152.1 N/mm², σ2 = 7.9 N/mm²
tan2θp = 2τxy/(σx−σy) = 1.5, so 2θp = 56.3°
τmax = 72.1 N/mm² at 45° to the principal planes

bank.q: Solve the previous stress state by drawing Mohr's circle to scale: locate the centre and radius, and read off the stresses on a plane at 30° to the x-face.
outline: Centre at (80, 0) N/mm², radius 72.1 N/mm²
Point A plotted at (120, 60)
Rotate diameter by 2θ = 60° in the correct sense
Read normal stress from the horizontal coordinate
Read shear stress from the vertical coordinate
Compare with values from the transformation equations

bank.q: A 45° strain rosette reads ε0 = 400×10⁻⁶, ε45 = 200×10⁻⁶ and ε90 = −100×10⁻⁶. Find εx, εy, γxy, the principal strains and their directions. Take E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.3.
outline: εx = ε0, εy = ε90
ε45 = (εx+εy)/2 + γxy/2 gives γxy
Principal strains from ε1,2 = (εx+εy)/2 ± √(((εx−εy)/2)² + (γxy/2)²)
tan2θp = γxy/(εx−εy)
Convert to stresses using plane stress Hooke's law

bank.q: A solid shaft of diameter d carries a bending moment M and a torque T. Obtain the principal stresses at the surface and find the diameter using the maximum shear stress theory with yield strength σy and factor of safety n.
outline: Bending stress σ = 32M/(πd³), torsional shear τ = 16T/(πd³)
Principal stresses = σ/2 ± √((σ/2)² + τ²)
τmax = √((σ/2)² + τ²)
Tresca: τmax ≤ σy/(2n)
Substitute and solve for d
Note the equivalent moment form √(M² + T²)

bank.q: A thin cylindrical pressure vessel of diameter D and thickness t has internal pressure p. Taking the surface element as biaxial, find the principal stresses and check the wall thickness by the von Mises theory with factor of safety n.
outline: Hoop stress σ1 = pD/(2t), axial σ2 = pD/(4t), shear zero
State that these are already principal stresses
von Mises σ′ = √(σ1² − σ1σ2 + σ2²)
Substitute to get σ′ = pD/(2t) × 0.866 approximately
Set σ′ ≤ σy/n and solve for t
Compare with the Tresca result

bank.q: Compare the maximum principal stress, maximum shear stress and maximum distortion energy theories. State the stress measure used, the safe-condition inequality and the material each suits.
outline: Rankine: σ1 compared with σy, brittle materials
Tresca: σ1 − σ2 compared with σy, ductile materials
von Mises: √(σ1² − σ1σ2 + σ2²) compared with σy, ductile materials
Behaviour under pure shear: Rankine and Tresca disagree, von Mises lies between
Tresca is conservative and simple; von Mises fits test data for metals
Hydrostatic stress causes no yielding in Tresca and von Mises

bank.q: For a state of pure shear τ, evaluate the stress measure predicted by each of the three theories and comment on which gives the safest design and at what cost.
outline: Principal stresses are +τ and −τ
Rankine measure = τ
Tresca measure = 2τ
von Mises measure = √3 τ ≈ 1.732τ
Rankine is unsafe here because it ignores the compressive principal stress
Tresca demands the largest section; von Mises is intermediate and best supported by tests

bank.q: A component is designed by one theory and fails in service under a combined bending and torsion load. Analyse the possible reasons and recommend a procedure for revising the design.
outline: Check whether the material is ductile or brittle and whether the theory matches
Recompute principal stresses including stress concentration
Check whether fatigue, not static yield, governs
Confirm the factor of safety definition used
Compare Tresca and von Mises diameters
Recommend combined-load equivalent stress with a fatigue factor

bank.q: Write the two-dimensional equilibrium equations and the strain-displacement relations. Explain why compatibility conditions are needed along with equilibrium to solve a plane stress problem.
outline: ∂σx/∂x + ∂τxy/∂y + X = 0 and ∂τxy/∂x + ∂σy/∂y + Y = 0
εx = ∂u/∂x, εy = ∂v/∂y, γxy = ∂u/∂y + ∂v/∂x
Three strains from two displacements means one compatibility link
∂²εx/∂y² + ∂²εy/∂x² = ∂²γxy/∂x∂y
Equilibrium alone gives stresses that may not be compatible with a continuous displacement field
Compatibility plus Hooke's law gives the governing equation in terms of stress or displacement

bank.q: Derive the strain transformation equations for plane strain and show why γ/2 appears where τ appeared in the stress equations.
outline: Start from displacement of a line element rotated by θ
Express εx′ and γx′y′ in terms of εx, εy, γxy and 2θ
Compare term by term with the stress equations
Identify ε ↔ σ and γ/2 ↔ τ
Explain that γ is an engineering shear strain equal to twice the tensor component
Note the invariant εx + εy = ε1 + ε2

glossary.def: A set of nine components, six independent in the symmetric case, that gives the stress on any plane through a point.
The normal to a principal plane, along which the shear stress vanishes.
A combination of stress or strain components that stays the same when the axes are rotated.
One third of the sum of the three normal stresses; also called hydrostatic or spherical stress.
The stress remaining after the mean stress is subtracted from each normal component.
A state in which the stresses on one pair of faces are zero, leaving σx, σy and τxy.
A state in which the strain in one direction is zero, leaving εx, εy and γxy.
A circle on the σ–τ plane whose points give the normal and shear stress on every plane through a point.
A point on the circle from which a line drawn parallel to a plane meets the circle at that plane's stress point.
A thin resistive foil bonded to a surface whose change in resistance measures the normal strain along its axis.
A group of three strain gauges set at fixed angles so the full plane strain state can be found.
The stress at which a material begins to deform permanently, usually taken at 0.2% offset for metals.
The ratio of the failure or yield strength to the working stress actually allowed in the part.
A single uniaxial stress that a chosen failure theory says is equally severe as the real combined stress state.
The boundary in principal-stress space that separates elastic from plastic behaviour.
A material that fractures with little plastic deformation before failure, such as cast iron.
A material that yields and stretches a large amount before fracture, such as mild steel.
The requirement that strains derived from a displacement field fit together without gaps or overlaps.
A force per unit volume acting throughout the material, such as self weight.
The force per unit area acting on a chosen plane through a point.
A local rise in stress near a hole, notch or sudden change of section.
The linear relation between stress and strain below the proportional limit, with constants E, G and ν.
